text: The value of the integral $\int\limits _{0}^{π/4}\frac{x\mathrm{d}x}{\sin ^{4}(2x)+\cos ^{4}(2x)}$ equals :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Take $I=\int\limits _{0}^{π/4}\frac{xdx}{\sin ^{4}(2x)+\cos ^{4}(2x)}$

Let $2x=t$

$2dx=dt$

$dx=\frac{dt}{2}$

$\begin{array}{l} I=\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{t/2\cdot 1/2dt}{\sin ^{4}t+\cos ^{4}t} \\  \\ I=\dfrac{1}{4}\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{tdt}{\sin ^{4}t+\cos ^{4}t} \\  \\ =\dfrac{1}{4}\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{\left (\frac{π}{2}-t\right )dt}{\sin ^{4}(π/2-t)+\cos ^{4}(π/2-t)} \\  \\ =\dfrac{1}{4}\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{\left (\frac{π}{2}-t\right )}{\sin ^{4}t+\cos ^{4}t} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} 2I=\dfrac{1}{4}\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{\frac{π}{2}}{\sin ^{4}t+\cos ^{4}t}dt \\  \\ 2I=\dfrac{π}{8}\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{dt}{\sin ^{4}t+\cos ^{4}t} \\  \\ 2I=\dfrac{π}{8}\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\dfrac{\sec ^{4}t}{1+\tan ^{4}t}dt \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \text{Put}\tan t=y \\  \\ \sec ^{2}tdt=dy \\  \\ 2I=\dfrac{π}{8}\int\limits _{0}^{\infty }\dfrac{\left (1+y^{2}\right )dy}{1+y^{4}} \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{8}\int\limits _{0}^{\infty }\dfrac{1+\frac{1}{y^{2}}}{y^{2}+\frac{1}{y^{2}}-2+2}dy \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{8}\int\limits _{0}^{\infty }\dfrac{\left (1+\frac{1}{y^{2}}\right )dy}{2+\left (y-\frac{1}{y}\right )^{2}} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \text{Put,}y-\dfrac{1}{y}=u \\  \\ 2I=\dfrac{π}{8}\int\limits _{-\infty }^{\infty }\dfrac{du}{2+u^{2}} \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{8\sqrt{2}}\left [\tan ^{-1}\dfrac{u}{\sqrt{2}}\right ]_{-\infty }^{\infty } \\  \\ =\dfrac{\sqrt{2}π^{2}}{16} \\  \\ \Rightarrow I=\dfrac{\sqrt{2}π^{2}}{32} \end{array}$
sourceReferences: ExamSIDE explanation for JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift

text: If $\mathrm{A}=\left [\begin{array}{ll} \sqrt{2} & 1 \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} \end{array}\right ],\mathrm{B}=\left [\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{array}\right ],\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{ABA}^{\mathrm{T}}$ and $\mathrm{X}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{C}^{2}\mathrm{A}$, then $\det \mathrm{X}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
The solution involves understanding matrix operations and properties such as multiplication, transpose, and determinant. Given $\mathrm{A}$, $\mathrm{B}$, and that $\mathrm{C}=\mathrm{ABA}^{\mathrm{T}}$, and $\mathrm{X}=\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{C}^{2}\mathrm{A}$, we find $\det \mathrm{X}$ as follows:

First, we express $|\mathrm{C}|$, the determinant of $\mathrm{C}$, in terms of the determinants of $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$, using the property that $|\mathrm{ABC}|=|\mathrm{A}|\cdot |\mathrm{B}|\cdot |\mathrm{C}|$:

$\begin{array}{ll} |\mathrm{C}| & =|\mathrm{ABA}^{\mathrm{T}}|=|\mathrm{A}|\cdot |\mathrm{B}|\cdot |\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}| \\  \\ =|\mathrm{A}|^{2}\cdot |\mathrm{B}|\text{since}|\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}|=|\mathrm{A}|. \end{array}$

Next, we find $|\mathrm{X}|$, using the property $|\mathrm{ABC}|=|\mathrm{A}|\cdot |\mathrm{B}|\cdot |\mathrm{C}|$ and substituting $|\mathrm{C}|$:

$\begin{array}{ll} |\mathrm{X}| & =|\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}\mathrm{C}^{2}\mathrm{A}|=|\mathrm{A}^{\mathrm{T}}|\cdot |\mathrm{C}|^{2}\cdot |\mathrm{A}| \\  \\ =|\mathrm{A}|^{2}\cdot |\mathrm{C}|^{2}. \end{array}$

Substituting the expression for $|\mathrm{C}|$ obtained earlier:

$\begin{array}{ll} |\mathrm{X}| & =|\mathrm{A}|^{2}\cdot (|\mathrm{A}|^{2}\cdot |\mathrm{B}|)^{2} \\  \\ =(|\mathrm{A}|^{3}\cdot |\mathrm{B}|)^{2}. \end{array}$

The determinants of $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ are calculated as:

$|A|=\left |\begin{array}{ll} \sqrt{2} & 1 \\ -1 & \sqrt{2} \end{array}\right |=2+1=3$

$|B|=\left |\begin{array}{ll} 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1 \end{array}\right |=1$
Finally, substituting these values into our expression for $|\mathrm{X}|$:

$\begin{array}{ll} |\mathrm{X}| & =(3^{3}\cdot 1)^{2} \\  \\ =729. \end{array}$

Therefore, $\det \mathrm{X}=729$.

If $\tan \mathrm{A}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}},\tan \mathrm{B}=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}$ and 

$\tan \mathrm{C}=\left (x^{-3}+x^{-2}+x^{-1}\right )^{1/2},0<\mathrm{A},\mathrm{B},\mathrm{C}<\frac{π}{2}$, then $\mathrm{A}+\mathrm{B}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the sum of two angles in terms of tangent, we can use the tangent addition formula: 

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{\tan A+\tan B}{1-\tan A\cdot \tan B}$

Let's compute $\tan (A+B)$ using the given $\tan A$ and $\tan B$: 

$\tan A=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x^{2}+x+1)}}$

$\tan B=\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}$

Now, we can apply the addition formula: 

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x2+x+1)}}+\frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x2+x+1}}}{1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{x(x2+x+1)}}\cdot \frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x2+x+1}}}$

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{\frac{1+\sqrt{x2}}{\sqrt{x(x2+x+1)}}}{1-\frac{1}{(x2+x+1)}}$

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{\frac{\sqrt{x2}+1}{\sqrt{x(x2+x+1)}}}{\frac{(x2+x+1)-1}{(x2+x+1)}}$

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{(x+1)\sqrt{(x^{2}+x+1)}}{(x^{2}+x)\sqrt{x}}$

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{(x+1)\sqrt{(x^{2}+x+1)}}{x(x+1)\sqrt{x}}$

$\tan (A+B)=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}{x^{3/2}}$

Let us first simplify $\tan \mathrm{C}$:

$\tan \mathrm{C}=\sqrt{x^{-3}+x^{-2}+x^{-1}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{x^{3}}+\frac{1}{x^{2}}+\frac{1}{x}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+x+x^{2}}{x^{3}}}=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+x+1}}{x^{3/2}}.$

We see that: 

$\tan (A+B)=\tan C$

Since tangent is positive and all the angles $A$, $B$, and $C$ are in the first quadrant, we can say that: 

$A+B=C$

Hence, the answer is: 

Option A : $C$

text: If $\mathrm{n}$ is the number of ways five different employees can sit into four indistinguishable offices where any office may have any number of persons including zero, then $\mathrm{n}$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the number of ways in which five different employees can be seated in four indistinguishable offices, we will use the concept of partitioning of an integer.

The problem is equivalent to partitioning the number 5 (representing the 5 different employees) into at most 4 parts (representing the 4 indistinguishable offices) where each part represents the number of employees in each office.

The partitions of 5 into at most 4 parts are as follows :

$(5,0,0,0)$ – One office has 5 employees, and the other three have none.

$(4,1,0,0)$ – One office has 4 employees, another one has 1, and the other two have none.

$(3,2,0,0)$ – One office has 3 employees, another one has 2, and the other two have none.

$(3,1,1,0)$ – One office has 3 employees, two have 1 each, and one has none.

$(2,2,1,0)$ – Two offices have 2 employees each, one has 1, and one has none.

$(2,1,1,1)$ – One office has 2 employees, and the other three have 1 each.

However, since the offices are indistinguishable, we must not count partitions that differ only by the order of the parts. This means that partitions like $(5,0,0,0)$, $(0,5,0,0)$, $(0,0,5,0)$, and $(0,0,0,5)$ all represent the same scenario and thus are counted as one.

So we end up with 6 distinct partition scenarios.

Now, for each partition, we need to find the number of ways to assign the employees according to each partition :

$(5,0,0,0)$ – All employees are in one office. There is 1 way to do this because the offices are indistinguishable.

$(4,1,0,0)$ - For the group with 4 employees, there are ${}^{5}C_{4}$ ways to choose which 4 out of the 5 will be together. Then the remaining employee is automatically assigned to the second office. So, there are ${}^{5}C_{4}$ ways for this partition.

$(3,2,0,0)$ - For the group with 3 employees, there are ${}^{5}C_{3}$ ways to choose them, and for the group with 2 employees, there are ${}^{2}C_{2}$ ways to choose them (which is essentially 1 way since the last 2 employees are automatically grouped). But the 2 offices these groups can occupy are indistinguishable, so we do not multiply by 2. So, there are ${}^{5}C_{3}$ ways for this partition.

$(3,1,1,0)$ - For the group with 3 employees, there are ${}^{5}C_{3}$ ways. Then we have two indistinguishable offices, each with 1 employee. The order does not matter as offices are indistinguishable. So, there are simply ${}^{5}C_{3}$ ways.

$(2,2,1,0)$ – For the first group of 2 employees, there are ${}^{5}C_{2}$ ways to choose them. For the next group of 2 employees, there are ${}^{3}C_{2}$ ways from the remaining 3. Then, the last employee is alone, and since the offices are indistinguishable, there are no further combinations to consider. However, we have double-counted since the two groups of two are indistinguishable. To adjust for this, we divide by 2. This gives us $\frac{{}^{5}C_{2}\cdot {}^{3}C_{2}}{2}$ ways.

$(2,1,1,1)$ - For the group with 2 employees, there are ${}^{5}C_{2}$ ways to choose them. The other three employees are each in their own office, with no further combinations since the offices are indistinguishable, so there are ${}^{5}C_{2}$ ways for this partition.

Let's compute these cases :

$(5,0,0,0)$ corresponds to $1$ way.

$(4,1,0,0)$ corresponds to ${}^{5}C_{4}=5$ ways.

$(3,2,0,0)$ corresponds to ${}^{5}C_{3}=10$ ways.

$(3,1,1,0)$ corresponds to ${}^{5}C_{3}=10$ ways.

$(2,2,1,0)$ corresponds to $\frac{{}^{5}C_{2}\cdot {}^{3}C_{2}}{2}=\frac{10\cdot 3}{2}=15$ ways.

$(2,1,1,1)$ corresponds to ${}^{5}C_{2}=10$ ways.

Adding up all the ways we get :

$1+5+10+10+15+10=51$

Therefore, the number of ways five different employees can sit into four indistinguishable offices ($\mathrm{n}$) is 51, which corresponds to Option C.

text: Let $\mathrm{S}=\{\mathrm{z}\in \mathrm{C}:|z-1|=1$ and $(\sqrt{2}-1)(z+\bar{z})-i(z-\bar{z})=2\sqrt{2}\}$. Let $z_{1},z_{2}\in \mathrm{S}$ be such that $|z_{1}|=\max _{z\in S}|z|$ and $|z_{2}|=\min _{z\in S}|z|$. Then $\left |\sqrt{2}z_{1}-z_{2}\right |^{2}$ equals :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let $z=x+iy$

$\begin{array}{l} |z-1|=1\Rightarrow |x+iy-1|=1 \\  \\ (x-1)^{2}+y^{2}=1.......(1) \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} (\sqrt{2}-1)(z+\bar{z})-i(z-\bar{z})=2\sqrt{2}\text{(Given)} \\  \\ (\sqrt{2}-1)(2x)-i(2iy)=2\sqrt{2} \\  \\ (\sqrt{2}-1)x+y=\sqrt{2}.........(2) \end{array}$

Solving (1) and (2), we get

$\begin{array}{l} (x-1)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}-(\sqrt{2}-1)x)^{2}=1 \\  \\ \left (x^{2}-2x+1\right )+2+(\sqrt{2}-1)^{2}x^{2}-2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}-1)x=1 \\  \\ x^{2}\left (1+(\sqrt{2}-1)^{2}\right )+x(-2-2\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{2}-1))+2=0 \\  \\ x^{2}(4-2\sqrt{2})+x(2\sqrt{2}-6)+2=0 \\  \\ x^{2}(2-\sqrt{2})+x(\sqrt{2}-3)+1=0 \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow x=1\text{and}x=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{2}}..........(3) \\  \\ \text{When}x=1,y=1\Rightarrow z_{2}=1+i \\  \\ \text{When}x=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{2}},y=\sqrt{2}-\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  \\ \Rightarrow z_{1}=\left (1+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )+\dfrac{i}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}$

Now,

$\begin{array}{l} \left |\sqrt{2}z_{1}-z_{2}\right |^{2} \\  \\ =\left |\left (\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+1\right )\sqrt{2}+i-(1+i)\right |^{2} \\  \\ =(\sqrt{2})^{2} \\  \\ =2 \end{array}$

text: Let $𝐒=\left \{x\in 𝐑:(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{x}+(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})^{x}=10\right \}$. Then the number of elements in $\mathrm{S}$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Notice that $(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})$ and $(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})$ are reciprocals of each other because :

$(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})=3-2=1$

Using the Reciprocal Property :

This means $(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})^{x}=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{x}}$

Let  $a=(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{x}$. The equation given in the problem becomes :

 $a+\frac{1}{a}=10$

Simplifying

Multiplying both sides by *a*, we get a quadratic equation :

 $a^{2}+1=10a$

 $a^{2}-10a+1=0$

Solving the Quadratic

Using the quadratic formula, we find :

 $a=\frac{10\pm \sqrt{96}}{2}=5\pm 2\sqrt{6}$

Possible values of x

Since $a=(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{x}$, we have two cases :

$(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{x}=5+2\sqrt{6}$ = $(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{2}$. There is one real solution for x in this case which is x = 2.

$(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{x}=5-2\sqrt{6}$ = $(\sqrt{3}-\sqrt{2})^{2}=\frac{1}{(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{2}}$ = $(\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{2})^{-2}$. There is one real solution for x in this case which is x = - 2.

Conclusion

There are two real solutions for *x*. Therefore, the number of elements in the set S is 2. This corresponds with option (C).

text: The area enclosed by the curves $xy+4y=16$ and $x+y=6$ is equal to :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$xy+4y=16$ gives $y=\dfrac{16}{x+4}$, a rectangular hyperbola with asymptote $x=-4$; the line is $y=6-x$.

Intersections: $(6-x)(x+4)=16\Rightarrow x^{2}-2x-8=0\Rightarrow x=-2,4$, i.e. the points $(-2,8)$ and $(4,2)$.


[IMG]

On $[-2,4]$ the line lies above the hyperbola (at $x=0$: $6>4$).

$A=\int\limits _{-2}^{4}\left (6-x-\frac{16}{x+4}\right )dx=\left [6x-\frac{x^{2}}{2}-16\ln (x+4)\right ]_{-2}^{4}$

$A=(24-8)-(-12-2)-16(\ln 8-\ln 2)=30-16\ln 4=30-32\log _{e}2$

Hence, the correct option is (C).

text:
Let $f:𝐑\to 𝐑$ and $g:𝐑\to 𝐑$ be defined as 

$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} \log _{\mathrm{e}}x, & x>0 \\ \mathrm{e}^{-x}, & x\leq 0 \end{array} \right.$ and 

$g(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} x, & x⩾0 \\ \mathrm{e}^{x}, & x<0 \end{array} \right.$. Then, gof : $𝐑\to 𝐑$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
For $x\leq 0$: $f(x)=e^{-x}\geq 1$, so $g(f(x))=e^{-x}$, which takes every value in $[1,\infty )$.

For $0<x<1$: $f(x)=\ln x<0$, so $g(f(x))=e^{\ln x}=x$, which takes the values in $(0,1)$.

For $x\geq 1$: $f(x)=\ln x\geq 0$, so $g(f(x))=\ln x$, which takes every value in $[0,\infty )$.

$g(f(x))=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} e^{-x}, & x\leq 0 \\ x, & 0<x<1 \\ \ln x, & x\geq 1 \end{array} \right.$

The value $2$ is taken at $x=-\ln 2$ and at $x=e^{2}$, so $g\circ f$ is not one-one.

The range is $[0,\infty )\neq \mathrm{ℝ}$, since no negative value is taken, so $g\circ f$ is not onto.

Hence, the correct option is (B).

text:
For $0<θ<π/2$, if the eccentricity of the hyperbola 

$x^{2}-y^{2}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ=5$ is $\sqrt{7}$ times eccentricity of the

 ellipse $x^{2}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ+y^{2}=5$, then the value of $θ$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the value of $θ$, we need to determine the relationship between the eccentricities of the given hyperbola and ellipse. Let's start by writing down the standard forms of ellipse and hyperbola and then relate them to the given equations.

The standard form of an ellipse is:

$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

The eccentricity $e$ of an ellipse is given by:

$e=\sqrt{1-\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}}\text{for}a>b$

For the given ellipse:

$x^{2}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ+y^{2}=5$

We can compare it with the standard form by writing it as:

$\frac{x^{2}}{\frac{5}{\mathrm{cosec}2θ}}+\frac{y^{2}}{5}=1$

From this we have $a^{2}=\frac{5}{\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ}$ and $b^{2}=5$. The eccentricity of the ellipse (let's call it $e_{1}$) is:

$e_{1}=\sqrt{1-\frac{a^{2}}{5}}=\sqrt{1-\frac{\frac{5}{\mathrm{cosec}2θ}}{5}}=\sqrt{1-\sin ^{2}θ}=\cos θ$

The standard form of a hyperbola is:

$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

The eccentricity $e$ of a hyperbola is given by:

$e=\sqrt{1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}}$

For the given hyperbola:

$x^{2}-y^{2}\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ=5$

We can rewrite it as:

$\frac{x^{2}}{5}-\frac{y^{2}}{\frac{5}{\mathrm{cosec}2θ}}=1$

From this we have $a^{2}=5$ and $b^{2}=\frac{5}{\mathrm{cosec}^{2}θ}$. The eccentricity of the hyperbola (let's call it $e_{2}$) is:

$e_{2}=\sqrt{1+\frac{\frac{5}{\mathrm{cosec}2θ}}{5}}=\sqrt{1+\sin ^{2}θ}$

According to the question the eccentricity of the hyperbola is $\sqrt{7}$ times the eccentricity of the ellipse, so we can write:

$e_{2}=\sqrt{7}\cdot e_{1}$

Substitute $e_{1}$ and $e_{2}$ from the above:

$\sqrt{1+\sin ^{2}θ}=\sqrt{7}\cdot \cos θ$

Square both sides to eliminate the square root:

$1+\sin ^{2}θ=7\cdot \cos ^{2}θ$

$1+\sin ^{2}θ=7\cdot (1-\sin ^{2}θ)$

$1+\sin ^{2}θ=7-7\cdot \sin ^{2}θ$

$8\cdot \sin ^{2}θ=6$

$\sin ^{2}θ=\frac{6}{8}=\frac{3}{4}$

$\sin θ=\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

Looking at the options provided and knowing the sine values for common angles, we can see that $\sin θ=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$ corresponds to $θ=\frac{π}{3}$.

The correct answer is:

Option C.

$\frac{π}{3}$

Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation 

$\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=2x(x+y)^{3}-x(x+y)-1,y(0)=1$.

Then, $\left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+y\left (\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )\right )^{2}$ equals :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Put $x+y=t$, so $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=\dfrac{dt}{dx}-1$ and the equation becomes

$\dfrac{dt}{dx}-1=2xt^{3}-xt-1\Rightarrow \dfrac{dt}{dx}=x\left (2t^{3}-t\right )$

Separating variables, $\dfrac{t~dt}{t^{2}(2t^{2}-1)}=xdx$. Putting $t^{2}=z$, $2tdt=dz$:

$\dfrac{1}{2}\int \dfrac{dz}{z(2z-1)}=\int xdx$

By partial fractions, $\dfrac{1}{z(2z-1)}=\dfrac{2}{2z-1}-\dfrac{1}{z}$, so

$\dfrac{1}{2}(\ln |2z-1|-\ln |z|)=\dfrac{x^{2}}{2}+c\Rightarrow \ln \left |\dfrac{2z-1}{z}\right |=x^{2}+2c$

At $x=0$, $y=1$: $t=1$ and $z=1$, so $\ln 1=2c$, giving $c=0$. Since $\dfrac{2z-1}{z}=1>0$ at $x=0$,

$\dfrac{2z-1}{z}=e^{x^{2}}\Rightarrow 2-\dfrac{1}{z}=e^{x^{2}}\Rightarrow (x+y)^{2}=z=\dfrac{1}{2-e^{x^{2}}}$

At $x=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$, $x^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}$:

$\left (\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+y\left (\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )\right )^{2}=\dfrac{1}{2-\sqrt{e}}$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

Let $f:𝐑\to 𝐑$ be defined as :

$f(x)=\left \{\begin{array}{ll} \frac{a-b\cos 2x}{x^{2}}; & x<0 \\  \\ x^{2}+cx+2; & 0\leq x\leq 1 \\  \\ 2x+1; & x>1 \end{array} \right.$

sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Continuity at $x=1$: $f(1)=1+c+2=3+c$ and $\lim _{x\to 1^{+}}(2x+1)=3$, so $c=0$.

Continuity at $x=0$: $f(0)=2$. As $x\to 0^{-}$ the denominator $x^{2}\to 0$, so the numerator must also vanish, giving $a=b$. Then

$\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}\dfrac{b(1-\cos 2x)}{x^{2}}=\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}\dfrac{2b\sin ^{2}x}{x^{2}}=2b=2$

so $a=b=1$.

At $x=0$: for $x<0$, $f(x)=\dfrac{2\sin ^{2}x}{x^{2}}=2-\dfrac{2x^{2}}{3}+\ldots$, so $f^{'}(0^{-})=\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}\dfrac{f(x)-2}{x}=0$; for $0\leq x\leq 1$, $f(x)=x^{2}+2$, so $f^{'}(0^{+})=0$. Hence $f$ is differentiable at $x=0$.

At $x=1$: $f^{'}(1^{-})=2x\left |_{x=1}=2 \right.$ and $f^{'}(1^{+})=2$. Hence $f$ is differentiable at $x=1$.

Each piece is differentiable on its own interval, so $m=0$ and

$m+a+b+c=0+1+1+0=2$

Hence, the correct option is (D).

text: Let $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1,\mathrm{a}>\mathrm{b}$ be an ellipse, whose eccentricity is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and the length of the latus rectum is $\sqrt{14}$. Then the square of the eccentricity of $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given the ellipse $\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}+\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$ with $a>b$, the eccentricity $e$ is given by the formula:

$e=\sqrt{1-\left (\frac{b}{a}\right )^{2}}$

It is provided that the eccentricity $e$ is $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ (given), so we can equate the two expressions for eccentricity:

$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}=\sqrt{1-\left (\frac{b}{a}\right )^{2}}$

Squaring both sides to eliminate the square root gives:

$\frac{1}{2}=1-\left (\frac{b}{a}\right )^{2}$

$\left (\frac{b}{a}\right )^{2}=1-\frac{1}{2}$

$\left (\frac{b}{a}\right )^{2}=\frac{1}{2}$

Taking the square root on both sides:

$\frac{b}{a}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

$a=b\sqrt{2}$

Now, for the ellipse, the length of the latus rectum is given by the formula:

$\text{Length of Latus Rectum (L)}=\frac{2b^{2}}{a}$

It's provided that the length of the latus rectum $L$ is $\sqrt{14}$, so substitute the known values to find $b$:

$\sqrt{14}=\frac{2b^{2}}{b\sqrt{2}}=\frac{2b}{\sqrt{2}}$

$b\sqrt{2}=\sqrt{14}$

$b^{2}=\frac{14}{2}$

$b^{2}=7$

And since $a=b\sqrt{2}$, we can find $a^{2}$:

$a^{2}=(b\sqrt{2})^{2}$

$a^{2}=7\cdot 2$

$a^{2}=14$

Now we have an ellipse with $a^{2}=14$ and $b^{2}=7$. The equation of a hyperbola similar to the given ellipse but with the terms subtracted is:

$\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}}-\frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}}=1$

For the hyperbola, the square of the eccentricity $e^{'}$ is given by:

$(e^{'})^{2}=1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}$

Substitute the values we've found for $a^{2}$ and $b^{2}$ into the formula for the square of the hyperbola's eccentricity:

$(e^{'})^{2}=1+\frac{b^{2}}{a^{2}}$

$(e^{'})^{2}=1+\frac{7}{14}$

$(e^{'})^{2}=1+\frac{1}{2}$

$(e^{'})^{2}=\frac{3}{2}$

Therefore, the square of the eccentricity of the hyperbola is $\frac{3}{2}$, which corresponds to option C.

text: Let $3,a,b,c$ be in A.P. and $3,a-1,b+1,c+9$ be in G.P. Then, the arithmetic mean of $a,b$ and $c$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Since $3,a,b,c$ are in arithmetic progression (A.P.), the common difference can be calculated using the term $a$ (the second term) as follows:

$d=a-3$

The nth term of an A.P. is given by the formula:

$T_{n}=a+(n-1)d$

So, using this formula, we can express $b$ and $c$ in terms of $a$ and $d$:

$b=a+d$

$c=a+2d$

Substituting $d=a-3$ into these expressions:

$b=a+(a-3)$

$c=a+2(a-3)$

Therefore:

$b=2a-3$

$c=3a-6$

Now, let's consider that $3,a-1,b+1,c+9$ are in geometric progression (G.P.). For terms in a G.P., the ratio (common ratio, r) between consecutive terms is constant. So:

$\frac{a-1}{3}=\frac{b+1}{a-1}=\frac{c+9}{b+1}$

Now, we will establish the relation between the terms using the property of G.P.:

$\frac{a-1}{3}=\frac{b+1}{a-1}$

$(a-1)^{2}=3(b+1)$

$a^{2}-2a+1=3b+3$

Substituting $b=2a-3$, we get:

$a^{2}-2a+1=3(2a-3)+3$

$a^{2}-2a+1=6a-9+3$

$a^{2}-8a+7=0$

Solving this quadratic equation:

$(a-7)(a-1)=0$

Hence, $a=7$ or $a=1$. However, if $a=1$, the terms $3,a-1,b+1,c+9$ cannot form a G.P. as it would involve division by zero. Therefore, $a=7$. We use this value to find $b$ and $c$:

$b=2a-3=2(7)-3=14-3=11$

$c=3a-6=3(7)-6=21-6=15$

Now we can find the arithmetic mean ($A$) of $a$, $b$, and $c$:

$A=\frac{a+b+c}{3}$

$A=\frac{7+11+15}{3}$

$A=\frac{33}{3}$

$A=11$

Hence, the arithmetic mean of $a$, $b$, and $c$ is $11$, which corresponds to Option D.

text:
If the shortest distance between the lines 

$\frac{x-λ}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$ and $\frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$ is 1 , then the sum of all possible values of $λ$ is :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Given the two lines:

$L_{1}:\frac{x-λ}{-2}=\frac{y-2}{1}=\frac{z-1}{1}$

$L_{2}:\frac{x-\sqrt{3}}{1}=\frac{y-1}{-2}=\frac{z-2}{1}$

We observe that these lines are not parallel as their directional vectors are not proportional. The directional vector for $L_{1}$ is $(-2,1,1)$ and for $L_{2}$ is $(1,-2,1)$. The shortest distance between two skew (non-intersecting and non-parallel) lines in the three-dimensional space is along the line that is perpendicular to both lines. This implies we can find a vector that is perpendicular to both directional vectors by taking their cross product.

The directional vector for $L_{1}$ is $d_{1}=\langle -2,1,1\rangle$, and for $L_{2}$ is $d_{2}=\langle 1,-2,1\rangle$. The cross product of $d_{1}$ and $d_{2}$, which will be perpendicular to both lines, is given by:

$d=d_{1}\times d_{2}=\left |\begin{array}{lll} 𝐢 & 𝐣 & 𝐤 \\ -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1 \end{array}\right |$

Expanding the determinate gives:

$d=𝐢((1)(1)-(1)(-2))-𝐣((-2)(1)-(1)(1))+𝐤((-2)(-2)-(1)(1))$

$d=𝐢(1+2)-𝐣(-2-1)+𝐤(4-1)$

$d=3𝐢+3𝐣+3𝐤$

$d=\langle 3,3,3\rangle$

The shortest distance $D$ between the two lines can then be given by the formula:

$D=\frac{|(𝐚_{𝟐}-𝐚_{𝟏})\cdot d|}{\|d\|}$

Where $𝐚_{𝟏}$ and $𝐚_{𝟐}$ are position vectors to any points on line $L_{1}$ and line $L_{2}$, respectively, and '$\cdot$' denotes the dot product.

From the lines' equations, we can choose a point on each line (when the parameter is zero). Thus, for $L_{1}$, let's choose the point $A(λ,2,1)$, and for $L_{2}$, let's choose the point $B(\sqrt{3},1,2)$. These points correspond to the vectors $𝐚_{𝟏}=\langle λ,2,1\rangle$ and $𝐚_{𝟐}=\langle \sqrt{3},1,2\rangle$, respectively.

The vector $𝐚_{𝟐}-𝐚_{𝟏}$ is:

$𝐚_{𝟐}-𝐚_{𝟏}=\langle \sqrt{3},1,2\rangle -\langle λ,2,1\rangle$

$𝐚_{𝟐}-𝐚_{𝟏}=\langle \sqrt{3}-λ,1-2,2-1\rangle$

$𝐚_{𝟐}-𝐚_{𝟏}=\langle \sqrt{3}-λ,-1,1\rangle$

We can now substitute this, along with $d$, into the distance formula:

$D=\frac{\left |(\langle \sqrt{3}-λ,-1,1\rangle )\cdot \langle 3,3,3\rangle \right |}{\|\langle 3,3,3\rangle \|}$

$D=\frac{\left |3(\sqrt{3}-λ)+3(-1)+3(1)\right |}{\sqrt{3^{2}+3^{2}+3^{2}}}$

$D=\frac{\left |3\sqrt{3}-3λ-3+3\right |}{\sqrt{27}}$

$D=\frac{\left |3\sqrt{3}-3λ\right |}{3\sqrt{3}}$

$D=\frac{\left |\sqrt{3}-λ\right |}{\sqrt{3}}$

Given that the shortest distance $D$ between the lines is 1, we can equate the above result to 1, and solve for $λ$:

$\frac{\left |\sqrt{3}-λ\right |}{\sqrt{3}}=1$

$\left |\sqrt{3}-λ\right |=\sqrt{3}$

This absolute value equation gives us two possible cases:

Case 1: $\sqrt{3}-λ=\sqrt{3}$, which gives $λ=0$.

Case 2: $\sqrt{3}-λ=-\sqrt{3}$, which gives $λ=2\sqrt{3}$.

Therefore, the sum of all possible values of $λ$ is:

$λ_{sum}=λ_{1}+λ_{2}=0+2\sqrt{3}=2\sqrt{3}$

Hence, option B ($2\sqrt{3}$) is the correct answer.

text: Let $3,7,11,15,\ldots ,403$ and $2,5,8,11,\ldots ,404$ be two arithmetic progressions. Then the sum, of the common terms in them, is equal to $___________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To find the common terms in the two given arithmetic progressions (AP), we need to first identify the common difference for each sequence and then find the sequence that represents their overlap by employing the concept of least common multiple (LCM).

The first AP is:

$3,7,11,15,\ldots ,403$

The common difference ($d_{1}$) for the first AP can be calculated by subtracting the first term from the second term:

$d_{1}=7-3=4$

The second AP is:

$2,5,8,11,\ldots ,404$

The common difference ($d_{2}$) for the second AP is:

$d_{2}=5-2=3$

To find the terms common to both sequences, we need to find a term that appears in both sequences. Any common term must be of the form $3+4k$ and $2+3l$ for some integers $k$ and $l$. We want to find when these two forms will give us the same number, so we set them equal to each other:

$3+4k=2+3l$

Rearranging the terms gives us:

$4k-3l=2-3$

This simplifies to:

$4k-3l=-1.......(1)$

The solutions to equation $(1)$ will give us the common terms. Notice this is a Diophantine equation (A Diophantine equation is a polynomial equation, usually with two or more variables,) and has an infinite number of solutions. Let's find one such solution. We can see that:

$k=1\text{yields}4(1)-3l=-1⟹4-3l=-1⟹3l=5⟹l=1\frac{2}{3}$

This is not an integer solution for $l$, so $k=1$ does not work. Trying $k=2$ gives:

$4(2)-3l=-1⟹8-3l=-1⟹3l=9⟹l=3$

Now we've found integers $k=2$ and $l=3$ that satisfy the equation. The corresponding term in both sequences would be:

$3+4(2)=3+8=11\text{and}2+3(3)=2+9=11$

Since $11$ is a common term, we can assert that every common term in both APs will be of the form $11+m(4\times 3)$, where $m$ is a non-negative integer, and $4\times 3=12$ is the LCM of the common differences of the two APs. Thus, the general form for the common terms would be:

$11+12m$

Now we are to find all terms that are common up to $403$ in the first sequence and up to $404$ in the second sequence. Because the first sequence doesn't exceed $403$, we'll use this as our limit:

$11+12m\leq 403$

To find the largest possible integer value for $m$, we solve the inequality:

$12m\leq 403-11$

$12m\leq 392$

$m\leq 32\frac{2}{3}$

Since $m$ has to be an integer, the largest possible value for $m$ is $32$. Therefore, the common terms are generated by $m=0,1,2,\ldots ,32$. There are $32+1=33$ terms in total.

We will now sum these up. The sum of an AP is given by the formula:

$S=\frac{n}{2}(a_{1}+a_{n})$

Where $S$ is the sum, $n$ is the number of terms, $a_{1}$ is the first term, and $a_{n}$ is the last term. Using the formula:

$S=\frac{33}{2}(11+(11+12\times 32))$

$S=\frac{33}{2}(11+11+384)$

$S=\frac{33}{2}(11+11+384)$

$S=\frac{33}{2}(406)$

$S=33\times 203$

$S=6699$

Therefore, the sum of the common terms in the two arithmetic progressions is 6699.

text: Let $\{x\}$ denote the fractional part of $x$ and $f(x)=\frac{\cos ^{-1}\left (1-\{x\}^{2}\right )\sin ^{-1}(1-\{x\})}{\{x\}-\{x\}^{3}},x\neq 0$. If $\mathrm{L}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ respectively denotes the left hand limit and the right hand limit of $f(x)$ at $x=0$, then $\frac{32}{π^{2}}\left (\mathrm{L}^{2}+\mathrm{R}^{2}\right )$ is equal to $___________$.

solution.body:
Finding right hand limit

R = $\begin{array}{l} \lim _{x\to 0^{+}}f(x)=\lim _{h\to 0}f(0+h)=\lim _{h\to 0}f(h) \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\lim _{h\to 0}\dfrac{\cos ^{-1}\left (1-h^{2}\right )\sin ^{-1}(1-h)}{h(1-h^{2})} \\  \\ =\lim _{\mathrm{h}\to 0}\dfrac{\cos ^{-1}\left (1-\mathrm{h}^{2}\right )}{\mathrm{h}}\left (\dfrac{\sin ^{-1}1}{1}\right ) \end{array}$

Let $\cos ^{-1}\left (1-h^{2}\right )=θ\Rightarrow \cos θ=1-h^{2}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\dfrac{π}{2}\lim _{θ\to 0}\dfrac{θ}{\sqrt{1-\cos θ}} \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{2}\lim _{θ\to 0}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos θ}{θ^{2}}}} \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{2}\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1/2}} \\  \\ \therefore \mathrm{R}=\dfrac{π}{\sqrt{2}} \end{array}$

Now finding left hand limit

$\begin{array}{l} L=\lim _{x\to 0^{-}}f(x)=\lim _{h\to 0}f(-h) \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\lim _{h\to 0}\dfrac{\cos ^{-1}\left (1-\{-h\}^{2}\right )\sin ^{-1}(1-\{-h\})}{\{-h\}-\{-h\}^{3}} \\  \\ =\lim _{h\to 0}\dfrac{\cos ^{-1}\left (1-(-h+1)^{2}\right )\sin ^{-1}(1-(-h+1))}{(-h+1)-(-h+1)^{3}} \\  \\ =\lim _{h\to 0}\dfrac{\cos ^{-1}\left (-h^{2}+2h\right )\sin ^{-1}h}{(1-h)(1-(1-h)^{2})} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} =\lim _{h\to 0}\left (\dfrac{π}{2}\right )\dfrac{\sin ^{-1}h}{(1-(1-h)^{2})} \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{2}\lim _{h\to 0}\left (\dfrac{\sin ^{-1}h}{-h^{2}+2h}\right ) \\  \\ =\dfrac{π}{2}\lim _{h\to 0}\left (\dfrac{\sin ^{-1}h}{h}\right )\left (\dfrac{1}{-h+2}\right ) \\  \\ L=\dfrac{π}{4} \end{array}$

$\begin{array}{l} \dfrac{32}{π^{2}}\left (\mathrm{L}^{2}+\mathrm{R}^{2}\right )=\dfrac{32}{π^{2}}\left (\dfrac{π^{2}}{2}+\dfrac{π^{2}}{16}\right ) \\  \\ =16+2 \\  \\ =18 \end{array}$

text: Let $\mathrm{P}=\{\mathrm{z}\in \mathrm{ℂ}:|z+2-3i|\leq 1\}$ and $\mathrm{Q}=\{\mathrm{z}\in \mathrm{ℂ}:z(1+i)+\bar{z}(1-i)\leq -8\}$. Let in $\mathrm{P}\cap \mathrm{Q}$, $|z-3+2i|$ be maximum and minimum at $z_{1}$ and $z_{2}$ respectively. If $|z_{1}|^{2}+2|z_{2}|^{2}=α+β\sqrt{2}$, where $α,β$ are integers, then $α+β$ equals $_____________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
$P$ is the disc $(x+2)^{2}+(y-3)^{2}\leq 1$, of centre $C(-2,3)$ and radius 1.

With $z=x+iy$: $z(1+i)+\bar{z}(1-i)=2\mathrm{Re}\left (z(1+i)\right )=2(x-y)$, so $Q$ is $x-y\leq -4$, the side of $L_{2}:x-y+4=0$ that contains $C$ (as $-2-3=-5\leq -4$). The distance of $C$ from $L_{2}$ is $\dfrac{|-2-3+4|}{\sqrt{2}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<1$, so $L_{2}$ cuts the disc.

$|z-3+2i|$ is the distance of $z$ from $A(3,-2)$. The line $AC$ is $L_{1}:x+y=1$, which is perpendicular to $L_{2}$.

The point of the disc farthest from $A$ lies on $AC$ beyond $C$, at distance 1 from $C$ in the direction $\dfrac{(-1,\qquad 1)}{\sqrt{2}}$:

$z_{1}=\left (-2-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}},3+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )$

and it satisfies $x-y=-5-\sqrt{2}\leq -4$, so it lies in $P\cap Q$.

$A$ is outside $Q$ ($3+2=5>-4$), so no point of $Q$ is nearer to $A$ than the foot of the perpendicular from $A$ to $L_{2}$. Solving $x+y=1$ and $x-y=-4$ gives this foot $z_{2}=\left (-\dfrac{3}{2},\dfrac{5}{2}\right )$, at distance $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}<1$ from $C$, so it lies in $P\cap Q$ and gives the minimum.

$|z_{1}|^{2}=\left (2+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )^{2}+\left (3+\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right )^{2}=\left (\frac{9}{2}+2\sqrt{2}\right )+\left (\frac{19}{2}+3\sqrt{2}\right )=14+5\sqrt{2}$

$2|z_{2}|^{2}=2\left (\frac{9}{4}+\frac{25}{4}\right )=17$

So $|z_{1}|^{2}+2|z_{2}|^{2}=31+5\sqrt{2}$, giving $α=31$, $β=5$ and $α+β=36$.

Hence, the answer is 36.

text: If $\int\limits _{-π/2}^{π/2}\frac{8\sqrt{2}\cos x\mathrm{d}x}{(1+\mathrm{e}^{\sin x})\left (1+\sin ^{4}x\right )}=απ+β\log _{\mathrm{e}}(3+2\sqrt{2})$, where $α,β$ are integers, then $α^{2}+β^{2}$ equals :
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
Let

$I=\int\limits _{-π/2}^{π/2}\frac{8\sqrt{2}\cos x}{(1+e^{\sin x})\left (1+\sin ^{4}x\right )}dx$

Replacing $x$ by $-x$ (the limits are symmetric) turns $\dfrac{1}{1+e^{\sin x}}$ into $\dfrac{e^{\sin x}}{1+e^{\sin x}}$, so adding the two forms of $I$:

$2I=\int\limits _{-π/2}^{π/2}\frac{8\sqrt{2}\cos x}{1+\sin ^{4}x}dx=2\int\limits _{0}^{π/2}\frac{8\sqrt{2}\cos x}{1+\sin ^{4}x}dx$

With $t=\sin x$, $I=8\sqrt{2}\int\limits _{0}^{1}\dfrac{dt}{1+t^{4}}$. Dividing numerator and denominator by $t^{2}$ and using $t^{2}+\dfrac{1}{t^{2}}=\left (t-\dfrac{1}{t}\right )^{2}+2=\left (t+\dfrac{1}{t}\right )^{2}-2$:

$I=4\sqrt{2}\int\limits _{0}^{1}\frac{\left (1+\frac{1}{t2}\right )dt}{\left (t-\frac{1}{t}\right )^{2}+2}-4\sqrt{2}\int\limits _{0}^{1}\frac{\left (1-\frac{1}{t2}\right )dt}{\left (t+\frac{1}{t}\right )^{2}-2}$

In the first integral $u=t-\dfrac{1}{t}$ runs from $-\infty$ to $0$:

$4\sqrt{2}\int\limits _{-\infty }^{0}\frac{du}{u^{2}+2}=4\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left [\tan ^{-1}\frac{u}{\sqrt{2}}\right ]_{-\infty }^{0}=4\cdot \frac{π}{2}=2π$

In the second integral $v=t+\dfrac{1}{t}$ runs from $\infty$ to $2$:

$4\sqrt{2}\int\limits _{\infty }^{2}\frac{dv}{v^{2}-2}=4\sqrt{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}\left [\ln \left |\frac{v-\sqrt{2}}{v+\sqrt{2}}\right |\right ]_{\infty }^{2}=2\ln \frac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}$

Since $\dfrac{2-\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{2}}=\dfrac{\left (2-\sqrt{2}\right )^{2}}{2}=3-2\sqrt{2}=\dfrac{1}{3+2\sqrt{2}}$, the second integral equals $-2\log _{e}\left (3+2\sqrt{2}\right )$.

Therefore $I=2π+2\log _{e}\left (3+2\sqrt{2}\right )$, so $α=2$, $β=2$ and $α^{2}+β^{2}=8$.

Hence, the answer is 8.

text:
Let $A=\{1,2,3,\ldots ,20\}$. Let $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ be two relations on $A$ such that 

$R_{1}=\{(a,b):b$ is divisible by $a\}$

$R_{2}=\{(a,b):a$ is an integral multiple of $b\}$.

Then, number of elements in $R_{1}-R_{2}$ is equal to $_____________$.
sourceReference: NTA JEE Main JEE Main 2024 (Online) 1st February Morning Shift via ExamSIDE (questions.examside.com)

solution.body:
To determine the number of elements in $R_{1}-R_{2}$, let's first articulate the meaning of both relations on set $A=\{1,2,3,\ldots ,20\}$:
$R_{1}$ includes pairs $(a,b)$ where $b$ is divisible by $a$. This includes pairs like $(1,1),(1,2),\ldots ,(1,20)$ for $1$; similar series for $2$ up to $(2,20)$ (excluding odd numbers); for $3$ up to $(3,18)$; and so on, reflecting the divisibility condition.

$\begin{array}{l} R_{1}:\left \{\begin{array}{l} (1,1),(1,2)\ldots ,(1,20), \\ (2,2),(2,4)\ldots ,(2,20), \\ (3,3),(3,6)\ldots ,(3,18), \\ (4,4),(4,8)\ldots ,(4,20), \\ (5,5)(5,10)\ldots ,(5,20), \\ (6,6),(6,12),(6,18),(7,7),(7,14), \\ (8,8),(8,16),(9,9),(9,18)(10,10), \\ (10,20),(11,11),(12,12)\ldots ,(20,20) \end{array}\right \{ \\  \\ n(R_{1})=66 \end{array}$

$R_{2}$ consists of pairs $(a,b)$ where $a$ is an integral multiple of $b$. Essentially, this relationship is the reverse of $R_{1}$. However, for the essence of $R_{1}-R_{2}$, the key overlap comes with pairs where $a=b$, since those are the pairs that clearly reflect both conditions identically (i.e., a number is always divisible by itself, and it is always a multiple of itself). There are 20 such pairs corresponding to each integer in $A$ from 1 to 20, resulting in the common elements between $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ (the intersection $R_{1}\cap R_{2}$) being 20 pairs.

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{R}_{1}\cap \mathrm{R}_{2}=\{(1,1),(2,2),\ldots (20,20)\} \\  \\ \mathrm{n}(\mathrm{R}_{1}\cap \mathrm{R}_{2})=20 \end{array}$
The difference $R_{1}-R_{2}$ seeks elements present in $R_{1}$ but not in $R_{2}$. Given that $R_{1}$ and $R_{2}$ share 20 elements that are identical, to find $R_{1}-R_{2}$, we subtract these 20 common elements from the total in $R_{1}$, resulting in $66-20=46$ pairs.

$\begin{array}{l} \mathrm{n}(\mathrm{R}_{1}-\mathrm{R}_{2})=\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{R}_{1})-\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{R}_{1}\cap \mathrm{R}_{2}) \\  \\ =\mathrm{n}(\mathrm{R}_{1})-20 \\  \\ =66-20 \\  \\ \mathrm{R}_{1}-\mathrm{R}_{2}=46\text{Pair} \end{array}$
